sense: for a loss or an injury

terms.grammar: phrase: sarciō, sarcīre, sarsī, sartum, with damnum, dētrīmentum or injūriam
evidence: Caes. BG 6.1: dētrīmentum in bellō acceptum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin says what is done: the loss is made good. Sarcīre is literally to patch or mend; Servius Sulpicius explained the Twelve Tables’ sarcītō as damnum solvitō, praestātō (Festus, in Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: compensate, make up for, balance one thing against another
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.5.33: damna ab aliquō aetātis frūctū compēnsāta (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to weigh things together. The noun compēnsātiō is the balancing of debts against credits in Roman law (the Digest), or in Cicero of one thing against another; not money paid for a loss.
In Caesar and Cicero an apology or excuse that is accepted; reparation for an injury from Tacitus on (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: summī labōrēs nostrī magnā compēnsātī glōriā
phrases.english: our very great labours were made up for by great glory

phrases.latin: luitur homicīdium certō pecorum numerō, recipitque satisfactiōnem ūniversa domus
phrases.english: for even a killing is atoned for with a fixed number of cattle, and the whole family accepts the compensation

sources: Lewis & Short: sarcio · Lewis & Short: compenso · Lewis & Short: compensatio · Lewis & Short: satisfactio
